title: KeepLoRA: Continual Learning with Residual Gradient Adaptation
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: General knowledge sits in the dominant subspace and specific knowledge in the residual one, so updating only the residual preserves old knowledge and keeps plasticity.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: two radar charts, then a circular radial bar chart
description: Three side-by-side plots. Panels (a) and (b) are radar charts of performance retention (50–100%) as the backbone keeps 100%, 95%, 90% or 85% of its principal singular components. Each polygon is a different color: teal, dark teal, orange and red. In (a), the general-domain datasets (Caltech101, Places, SUN397, ImageNet, CIFAR100) show polygons that stay close together and near the outer edge. In (b), the specific-domain datasets (Aircraft, Food, DTD, OxfordPets, EuroSAT, StanfordCars, Flowers) show the inner polygons collapsing sharply. Panel (c) is a circular bar chart comparing continual-learning methods. Dark blue bars show Last-task gain and light blue bars show Transfer degradation. The KeepLoRA and KeepLoRA+ bars sit at the top, and the numbers are printed on the bars.
caption: Analysis of model parameter subspaces and overall CL performance. In Fig. [ref] and [ref], we measure zero-shot performance after reconstructing attention weights using only the top principal singular components. While performance on general-domain datasets remains highly robust, performance on most specific-domain datasets degrades sharply as more low-energy components are removed. In Fig. [ref], the Last metric measures the accuracy gain on the final learned task relative to a zero-shot baseline, while Transfer measures the accuracy degradation on unseen tasks.
abstract: Continual learning for pre-trained vision-language models requires balancing three competing objectives: retaining pre-trained knowledge, preserving knowledge from a sequence of learned tasks, and maintaining the plasticity to acquire new knowledge. This paper presents a simple but effective approach called KeepLoRA to effectively balance these objectives. We first analyze the knowledge retention mechanism within the model parameter space and find that general knowledge is mainly encoded in the principal subspace, while task-specific knowledge is encoded in the residual subspace. Motivated by this finding, KeepLoRA learns new tasks by restricting LoRA parameter updates in the residual subspace to prevent interfering with previously learned capabilities. Specifically, we infuse knowledge for a new task by projecting its gradient onto a subspace orthogonal to both the principal subspace of pre-trained model and the dominant directions of previous task features. Our theoretical and empirical analyses confirm that KeepLoRA balances the three objectives and achieves state-of-the-art performance. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/MaolinLuo/KeepLoRA.
